prompt_free_text:
This paper presents a broad empirical study of task-specific knowledge distillation for natural language generation, centered on pseudo-target training under a “realistic” medium-resource setting with additional unlabeled data. The paper compares encoder-decoder and decoder-only architectures, studies pruning choices, evaluates several KD objectives, and then develops a family of pseudo-target augmentation strategies, culminating in the proposed Joint-Teaching method that mixes teacher- and student-generated pseudo-targets. The experiments span four English-to-English generation tasks and include an additional exploratory GPT-4-to-T5 setting without labeled data. Overall, the paper is ambitious, practically motivated, and contains several useful empirical findings. I found the work interesting and potentially valuable to practitioners, especially the emphasis on unlabeled task-specific data and practical inference metrics such as latency and throughput. At the same time, some of the central claims are stronger than what the evidence fully supports, and several methodological choices limit the scientific conclusiveness of the study.

The main strengths are clear. First, the paper addresses an important and underexplored regime: task-specific NLG distillation with moderate labeled data and abundant unlabeled inputs. This is indeed a realistic deployment scenario and is less studied than high-resource NMT-style sequence-level KD. Second, the paper is unusually comprehensive in scope. It does not only compare KD losses, but also architecture families, pruning strategies, pseudo-target generation choices, and the use of unlabeled data. Third, the practical orientation is commendable. Reporting latency and throughput in addition to parameter counts and FLOPs is useful, and the conclusion that decoder pruning is often preferable for autoregressive generation is intuitive and empirically relevant. Fourth, the pseudo-target results are genuinely interesting: multiple pseudo-targets, sampling-based generation, and unlabeled-data augmentation all appear to help substantially in the reported setup. Finally, the paper is generally well written and the motivation around exposure bias is thought-provoking, even if I am not fully convinced by the causal interpretation.

That said, my biggest concern is that the paper frames itself as a “systematic study,” but the experimental design is only partially systematic. The authors explicitly use a sequential stage-wise selection procedure, choosing one option at each stage based on average development performance and then carrying only that choice forward. This is understandable computationally, but it means later conclusions are conditional on earlier choices and may not hold under alternative combinations. For example, the conclusion that Logits KD is the best base objective is established before the strongest pseudo-target methods are introduced, but it is plausible that Noisy KD or Attention-Relations KD would interact differently with multiple sampled pseudo-targets or Joint-Teaching. Similarly, the superiority of sampling over beam search may depend on the chosen objective, student architecture, or number of pseudo-targets. Because the paper does not test interactions, several conclusions should be stated more cautiously as “best within this pipeline” rather than general recommendations.

A related issue is the aggregation methodology. Much of Table 3 reports “fraction of student-teacher gap closed,” averaged over metrics, datasets, and student-teacher pairs. This normalization is intuitive, but it can also be misleading. Gap-closure percentages can be unstable when the teacher-student gap is small, and averaging across heterogeneous metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore, and perplexity may obscure important differences. The paper occasionally acknowledges this, for example noting that Noisy KD’s wins are driven by perplexity, but the main narrative still relies heavily on aggregate percentages and win counts. I would have liked to see stronger statistical treatment: confidence intervals or bootstrap significance for key pairwise comparisons, per-task absolute scores in the main text rather than mostly in appendices, and perhaps rank-based summaries that are less sensitive to scale differences across metrics. As it stands, some improvements in development score are numerically small, and it is hard to judge robustness.

The architecture comparison between encoder-decoder and decoder-only models is useful but not fully controlled. The paper argues that encoder-decoder models outperform decoder-only models for task-specific conditional NLG, and the reported averages support that. However, the compared model families differ in more than architecture: pretraining objectives, tokenization, optimization history, and instruction-following suitability all vary across GPT-2/OPT versus T5/BART. The paper notes some parameter/FLOP comparability, but this does not eliminate confounds. Therefore, the conclusion should be softened from an architectural statement to an empirical observation about these model families under these fine-tuning conditions. A more convincing architecture claim would require closer matched comparisons or at least stronger discussion of confounding factors.

The pruning section is practically useful, and the decoder-pruning result is plausible. Still, the study only prunes one family, BART-6:6, using a single simple heuristic that keeps first and last layers. This is enough for a practical observation but not enough for a broad claim that decoder pruning is generally better. It may be true for these tasks and lengths, but the paper should emphasize that this is a limited comparison rather than a general pruning principle. It would also help to report whether the pruned students were re-tuned comparably and whether alternative pruning depths were considered.

The pseudo-target contributions are the strongest part of the paper. The evidence that unlabeled inputs help when paired with teacher-generated targets is compelling within the presented setup, and the gains are large enough to be practically meaningful. Likewise, the move from a single beam pseudo-target to multiple sampled pseudo-targets is a sensible and valuable extension of sequence-level KD. This part of the paper makes a concrete contribution beyond prior work. However, the theoretical framing around exposure bias is somewhat overstated. The paper repeatedly motivates pseudo-target training as mitigating exposure bias because the student conditions on teacher-generated histories rather than gold histories. This is plausible, but the experiments do not isolate exposure bias reduction from simpler explanations such as data augmentation, label smoothing-like regularization, or better support coverage of the teacher distribution. Figure 2 is suggestive, but it is only a single setup analysis on SQuAD17 and does not directly establish that exposure bias is the mechanism behind the observed gains. I would recommend reframing this as a motivating perspective rather than a demonstrated explanation.

The proposed Joint-Teaching method is interesting and probably the most novel algorithmic element. Training on both teacher- and student-generated pseudo-targets, with teacher logits supervising continuations on student prefixes, is a reasonable way to expose the student to its own induced contexts while retaining a stronger supervisory signal. The empirical gains over teacher-only or student-only pseudo-targets are encouraging. Still, the method raises several questions that are not fully answered. Why 50% student-generated pseudo-targets? Is this ratio tuned, and how sensitive are results to it? Are student pseudo-targets regenerated online every step, every epoch, or cached? How much additional training cost does Joint-Teaching incur relative to teacher-only pseudo-target training? Since the paper explicitly deprioritizes training cost, this omission is understandable, but for a method whose main novelty is in training dynamics, cost and implementation details matter. Also, the comparison is limited to a small set of alternatives; it would be useful to compare against scheduled sampling-style baselines or simpler curriculum variants to better support the claim that Joint-Teaching specifically addresses exposure bias.

The GPT-4 extreme setup is a nice addition, but it feels exploratory rather than integrated into the main contribution. The results are mixed, and the paper attributes this partly to tokenizer mismatch. That is plausible, but the section remains somewhat underdeveloped. Since the teacher is prompted with three demonstrations, the setup is not truly unlabeled in the strictest sense; it uses a few labeled exemplars in-context. More importantly, the inability to evaluate Joint-Teaching there means the section does not really test the paper’s full recipe. I would treat this as an interesting appendix-style case study rather than a core validation.

There are also some concerns about dataset choices and evaluation. The four tasks are diverse, which is good, but all are English-to-English and relatively short-output settings. The paper acknowledges this limitation. More importantly, one dataset, Shake7, is newly constructed by the authors. Since this dataset contributes to several strong gains, more transparency is needed in the main paper about its construction quality, split methodology, deduplication, and potential overlap or stylistic artifacts. For style transfer/simplification tasks, lexical overlap metrics can be especially problematic, so the reliance on BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore should be complemented by stronger task-specific evaluation or human judgments beyond the ART10 appendix. The human evaluation on ART10 is helpful, but it would be even more valuable on Shake7 or summarization, where pseudo-target diversity and sampling may affect fluency and faithfulness in ways not captured by automatic metrics.

Another methodological concern is fairness in computational comparisons. Latency and throughput are measured on a single RTX 4080, which is useful, but these numbers can depend heavily on batching, decoding parameters, sequence lengths, and implementation details. The paper says averages are over four tasks, but because input/output lengths differ substantially, averaged latency may hide important task-specific tradeoffs. Table 4 does provide per-dataset computational numbers, which helps. Still, for claims like “3.7x faster,” it would be useful to clarify whether decoding settings are identical across teacher and student and whether beam size or sampling parameters differ. Since pseudo-target generation methods are central to training but not inference, this mostly affects the architecture/pruning claims rather than the final deployment story.

I also found some presentation choices slightly confusing. The paper introduces eight stages, but stage numbering in the results sometimes merges or shifts concepts, and stage 7 appears to cover both sampling and Joint-Teaching in different places. The notation around “Dev” scores is not always transparent in the main text because the task-specific development metric differs by dataset and is relegated to the appendix. Since stage-wise model selection depends on these development scores, the exact criterion should be more prominent. There are also a few places where claims are stronger than the evidence, such as “first exposure bias perspective for KD” or “first study” statements, which should be made carefully unless the literature search is exhaustive.

Despite these criticisms, I think the paper has real merit. The empirical message that pseudo-target training can be substantially more effective when expanded beyond single beam outputs is important and likely to influence practice. The use of unlabeled task-specific inputs is especially compelling and underappreciated in NLG distillation. The paper’s practical recommendations—prefer encoder-decoder students for conditional NLG, prune decoder layers when targeting latency, combine logits KD with pseudo-targets, use multiple sampled pseudo-targets, and consider mixing teacher and student prefixes—form a coherent recipe that seems well supported within the tested regime.

To strengthen the paper, I would suggest several concrete improvements. First, temper the strongest general claims and clearly distinguish between broad principles and findings conditional on the chosen pipeline and datasets. Second, add statistical significance or uncertainty estimates for the key comparisons in Table 3 and report more absolute scores in the main paper. Third, provide more ablations for Joint-Teaching, especially the teacher/student mixing ratio, regeneration schedule, and training-cost overhead. Fourth, clarify the extent to which pseudo-target gains are due to exposure-bias mitigation versus generic augmentation by adding at least one targeted control, such as multiple gold paraphrase-like augmentations if available, or teacher-generated targets without logits supervision under matched data volume. Fifth, improve transparency around the Shake7 dataset and, if possible, include additional human evaluation on one more task. Finally, if space permits, a limited interaction study would greatly improve the “systematic” claim—for example, testing whether the sampling advantage holds under Noisy KD as well as Logits KD.

My overall assessment is positive but not unreservedly so. This is a useful and practically relevant empirical paper with one interesting new method and several strong experimental observations. Its main weakness is that the evidence does not fully justify some of the broader causal and general claims, and the stage-wise design limits how systematic the conclusions really are. If the authors moderate the claims and strengthen the analysis, I think the paper would make a worthwhile contribution.

I would lean toward acceptance at a venue that values careful empirical studies and practical guidance, though not as a definitive methodological breakthrough. The work is solid, informative, and likely to be useful, but it would benefit from tighter claims and deeper analysis of mechanisms and interactions.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper presents a broad empirical study of task-specific knowledge distillation for natural language generation under a medium-resource setting with additional unlabeled data. The authors compare encoder-decoder vs. decoder-only architectures, encoder vs. decoder pruning, several KD objectives, and a family of pseudo-target (PT) augmentation strategies. Their main proposal is to extend sequence-level KD by generating multiple PTs, including for unlabeled inputs, preferring sampling over beam search, and introducing Joint-Teaching, which applies word-level KD on PTs generated by both teacher and student. Across four English NLG tasks, they report that encoder-decoder models are preferable for task-specific fine-tuning, decoder pruning is better than encoder pruning, unlabeled PTs help substantially, multiple sampled PTs outperform single beam PTs, and Joint-Teaching yields the best average distilled performance. They also include a limited GPT-4 teacher experiment in a no-labeled-data setting.
strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: compressing NLG systems for deployment while leveraging unlabeled task-specific data, which is realistic and underexplored relative to standard high-resource KD setups.
The study is unusually broad, covering architecture choice, pruning, KD objectives, PT generation strategies, and a new Joint-Teaching variant across multiple tasks and two teacher-student pairs.
The empirical findings are practically actionable: use encoder-decoder students, prefer decoder pruning, combine logits KD with PTs, exploit unlabeled data, and generate multiple sampled PTs.
The paper evaluates both task quality and deployment-oriented efficiency metrics such as latency and throughput, which strengthens its practical relevance.

The proposed Joint-Teaching idea is intuitive and potentially useful: teacher supervision on student-generated prefixes is a reasonable way to address train-test mismatch in autoregressive generation.
The paper is generally transparent about limitations, including training cost, scope of tasks, and the constraints of using GPT-4 as a teacher.
weaknesses: The work is framed as a systematic study, but the experimental design is sequential and greedy: decisions are fixed stage-by-stage based on development performance, so interactions between choices are not rigorously explored and some conclusions may be path-dependent.
Many central claims are supported only empirically and on averages over a small set of tasks; the paper often generalizes beyond what the evidence strictly supports.

The exposure-bias motivation is suggestive rather than rigorous. The argument that PTs and Joint-Teaching mitigate exposure bias is not formally established, and the supporting analysis is limited to a single setup.

The main aggregate metric, fraction of student-teacher gap closed, can be unstable and hard to interpret when teacher-student gaps differ across tasks/metrics; averaging this quantity across heterogeneous metrics may obscure absolute performance differences.

The comparison of KD objectives may not be fully fair because methods have different computational budgets and possibly different sensitivity to hyperparameters, yet the paper advances one method based mainly on average dev score.
The GPT-4 extreme setup is too limited to strongly support transferability of the main conclusions; results are explicitly mixed and only two datasets are used.

Some novelty claims appear overstated, especially around being the first to discuss exposure bias in KD for NLG or to challenge mode-approximation PT generation; related areas such as scheduled sampling, imitation learning, and diverse decoding already touch adjacent ideas.
The paper relies heavily on automatic metrics such as BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore/PPL for diverse generation tasks, while human evaluation is only briefly mentioned for one dataset.
methodological_flaws: The stage-wise selection procedure introduces a methodological confound: because later experiments inherit earlier choices, the reported superiority of later components may depend on earlier fixed decisions. Without factorial ablations or interaction analysis, causal attribution to individual design choices is weaker than implied.

The use of the normalized metric (KD-S)/(T-S)% is problematic when T-S is small, as it can exaggerate gains or make comparisons across tasks and metrics unreliable. The paper does not discuss variance, confidence intervals, or robustness of this aggregate statistic.

The claim that multiple sampled PTs expose the student to a larger portion of the learnable distribution and therefore improve generalization is plausible but not scientifically demonstrated; no diversity quantification, calibration analysis, or controlled study isolates whether gains come from diversity, data multiplication, or regularization effects.

The exposure-bias argument for Joint-Teaching rests on the assumption that the teacher models P(y_i | x, y^S_{<i}) better than the student. Evidence is provided only via a single BLEU-based continuation analysis on one dataset/model pair, which is insufficient to validate the assumption generally.

The architecture comparison between encoder-decoder and decoder-only models is not fully controlled. Models differ not only in architecture but also in pretraining objectives, tokenization, scaling, and family-specific implementation details, so attributing gains primarily to architecture is scientifically too strong.

The pruning conclusion is based on one pruning heuristic applied to one model family (BART) with fixed retained layers. This does not justify a broad rule that decoder pruning is generally better than encoder pruning.
Empirical validity is weakened by limited reporting of statistical uncertainty. There are no significance tests or error bars for the many comparisons, despite many reported differences being modest.

The paper explicitly ignores training-time computational cost in the main evaluation, yet several proposed methods require substantial teacher generation and repeated student/teacher interaction. Since the paper advocates practical deployment recipes, omitting this cost weakens the methodological completeness of the comparison.
